endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Trained patient actors or representative individuals who could plausibly present as patients are directed to follow defined scenarios, with outputs evaluated against prospectively defined criteria.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The research and operational teams ran COMPOSER in silent mode before activation, used a phased go-live, and established a structured clinician feedback loop in which alert disposition (acted on, deferred, or overridden) was logged and reviewed by the development team to recalibrate thresholds and retrain staff where needed.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: A silent evaluation involves generating AI system output using production data, but not displaying that output to personnel who would take action as part of the system workflow.

endorsements.title: Machine learning models in clinical practice for the prediction of postoperative complications after major abdominal surgery
endorsements.quote: A prospective simulation study in which the predictive performance of a model is tested in addition to the regular local care without affecting its course would enable the correct calibration of the ML model.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in medicine: mitigating risks and maximizing benefits via quality assurance, quality control, and acceptance testing
endorsements.quote: In general, this step should be completed after the tool is installed but before clinical use to ensure clinical decisions are not influenced.

endorsements.title: Collaborative and Cooperative Hospital "In-House" Medical Device Development and Implementation in the AI Age: The European Responsible AI Development (EURAID) Framework Compatible With European Values
endorsements.quote: Since validation in real-world settings is still a bottleneck [ 97 ], prospective, noninterventional silent trials [ 98 , 99 ] (where AI is tested within the clinical pathway in real time without affecting patients) can enhance transparency and facilitate informed deployment decisions.

endorsements.title: Barriers and opportunities of scaling ambient AI scribes for clinical documentation across diverse healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: Translational trials that include a silent testing phase, wherein a model’s performance is evaluated prospectively in its clinical context without impacting patient care or workflow as the model output is not shown to end-users, may be warranted as part of the evaluation process before full implementation 41 , 42 .

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence and Enhanced Recovery After Surgery as Patient Safety Strategies for Perioperative Care in Resource-Limited Settings
endorsements.quote: In hospitals with limited data infrastructure, local validation may begin pragmatically through small-scale silent testing, clinician review of outputs, comparison with observed outcomes, documentation of false alerts and missed events, and staged use before full clinical integration.

endorsements.title: A Clinical-Operational Framework for Responsible Artificial Intelligence Use in Infection Risk Management Among Immunosuppressed Patients: A Technical Report
endorsements.quote: Implementation should be phased: definition of the clinical-operational problem, target population, supported decision, data sources, and foreseeable risks; retrospective validation and data quality review; silent-mode evaluation without modifying clinical decisions; supervised pilot testing with trained users; and gradual scaling conditioned on acceptable local performance, operational utility, and absence of safety signals.

endorsements.title: Clinical cognition in the age of cardiovascular AI
endorsements.quote: Silent trials, prospective validation, local calibration, bias assessment, drift monitoring, documentation of decisions, retraining rules, and retirement criteria should be considered part of the technology.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing AI-Enabled Cardiovascular Biomarkers: A Clinician-Centered Framework for Validation, Governance, and Workflow Integration
endorsements.quote: Workflow simulation, silent or shadow-mode testing, and early prospective evaluation can identify these failures before broad implementation [ 9 - 12 , 26 , 32 ].

evidence.title: Development and Validation of an Artificial Intelligence Predictive Model to Accelerate Antibiotic Therapy for Critical Ill Children with Sepsis in the Pediatric ED with Pediatric ICU Disposition
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity in silent implementation versus model testing
evidence.effect: During silent implementation (1,058 encounters), the SEPD model maintained similar sensitivity (85.29%) and specificity (60.45%) to those observed during model testing.
evidence.quote: During silent implementation, the SEPD model maintained similar sensitivity (85.29%) and specificity (60.45%) to those observed during model testing.

evidence.title: DEPLOYR: a technical framework for deploying custom real-time machine learning models into the electronic medical record
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Performance gap detected by shadow deployment on live EMR data
evidence.effect: Across 12 models, prospective AUROC was lower than retrospective, e.g., hemoglobin 0.88 vs 0.83, potassium 0.67 vs 0.60; authors recommend prospective silent-trial estimates for go decisions.
evidence.quote: Across our 12 laboratory predictions tasks, AUROC in our prospective test sets were generally several percentage points lower than what is seen retrospectively.
evidence.sample_unit: machine learning models (laboratory result classifiers) silently deployed

evidence.title: Development and validation of a machine learning model integrated with the clinical workflow for early detection of sepsis
evidence.outcome: Model performance after deployment compared with pre-operations performance
evidence.effect: Pre-operations sensitivity 92%, specificity 93%, FPR 7%; post-deployment sensitivity 91%, specificity 94%, FPR 6%, i.e. comparable performance.
evidence.quote: Following deployment, the model maintained comparable performance, with a sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 94%.

evidence.title: Review and reflections on live AI mammographic screen reading in a large UK NHS breast screening unit
evidence.outcome: AI silent-mode outputs compared with actual double-reader decisions before clinical use
evidence.effect: 9,547 cases; 1,135 positive discordant reviewed, 1 additional recall (no cancer); 8 cancers (8.79%) recalled by humans missed by AI; no additional cancers detected by AI.
evidence.quote: Having missed a significant number of cancers makes it unreliable and not safe to be used in clinical practice.

evidence.title: Real-world deployment and evaluation of PEri-operative AI CHatbot (PEACH): a large language model chatbot for peri-operative medicine
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of chatbot responses in silent deployment on real-world data versus guidelines and expert consensus
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 96.7% (232/240) across three iterations; updated PEACH 97.9% (235/240), significantly above 95% null (p = 0.018).
evidence.quote: The system was tested with a silent deployment using real-world data.

evidence.title: Predicting the Value of Radiology Artificial Intelligence Applications: Large-Scale Predeployment Evaluation of a Portfolio of Models
evidence.effect: Predeployment evaluation using local data agreed with real-world postdeployment value perceptions for 10 of 12 tasks.
evidence.quote: A validation survey indicated high agreement between predeployment predictions and real-world postdeployment value perceptions.

evidence.title: In vivo clinical effectiveness of artificial intelligence screening for acute coronary syndrome: testing real-world performance
evidence.outcome: Silent mode CDS decisions versus original model and actual human decisions
evidence.effect: CDS sensitivity 81.7% vs in vitro model 82.0% vs human 80.2%; specificity 67.3% vs 67.3% vs 67.4%; raw agreement 96.8%, Kappa 91.2%
evidence.quote: We found 96.8% raw agreement and a Kappa of 91.2% (95% CI 90.7% to 91.8%).

evidence.title: Prospective Shadow-Mode Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence Tool for Intracranial Aneurysm Detection on CT Angiography: Incremental Yield and Operational Impact
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.effect: Shadow-mode testing identified variable setting-specific metrics, informing clinical deployment decisions.
evidence.quote: The AI tool demonstrated favorable operational performance, supporting clinical deployment in real-world practice, although setting-specific metrics were variable.

evidence.title: Deployment of Real-time Natural Language Processing and Deep Learning Clinical Decision Support in the Electronic Health Record: Pipeline Implementation for an Opioid Misuse Screener in Hospitalized Adults
evidence.outcome: Silent-mode performance of deep learning screener on live EHR notes versus physician review
evidence.effect: Silent testing on 100 adult encounters showed sensitivity 93% (95% CI 66%-99%) and specificity 92% (95% CI 84%-96%), similar to published validation studies.
evidence.quote: On-site silent testing of the deep learning algorithm demonstrated a sensitivity of 93% (95% CI 66%-99%) and specificity of 92% (95% CI 84%-96%), similar to published validation studies.

evidence.title: Natural Language Processing - A Surveillance Stepping Stone to Identify Child Abuse
evidence.outcome: Silent-mode NLP outputs compared with actual clinician evaluation and guideline adherence on live notes
evidence.effect: Adherence to guideline-recommended evaluation was 63%. Seventy-three false triggers were found and used to refine the algorithm.
evidence.quote: Seventy-three cases falsely triggered the NLP, often due to errors in interpreting linguistic context.

evidence.title: Detecting changes in the performance of a clinical machine learning tool over time
evidence.effect: The model achieved an average AUC of 0.78 for predicting blood culture outcomes during real-time shadow evaluation.
evidence.quote: The average AUC for predicting BC outcomes was 0.78 (standard deviation (SD) = 0.02).

evidence.title: In vitro to in vivo translation of artificial intelligence for clinical use: screening for acute coronary syndrome to identify ST-elevation myocardial infarction
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Coding errors uncovered by silent-mode fidelity analysis on live data
evidence.effect: Silent pilot on live data found additional coding errors, which were corrected before clinical use.
evidence.quote: Additional coding errors were identified and were corrected.

evidence.title: Ensuring fair, safe, and interpretable artificial intelligence-based prediction tools in a real-world oncological setting
evidence.outcome: Model performance and behavior during 77-day silent deployment on live EHR data
evidence.effect: Overall AUC fell from 0.80 (test) to 0.76 (production), delta −0.04; calibration was maintained; silent deployment revealed an EHR data feed outage before clinical use.
evidence.quote: The reduced number of visits to the ED may have been a driving factor in our discrimination performance dropping slightly, on average, across the production assessment period (Fig. 4e ).

evidence.title: Detecting changes in the performance of a clinical machine learning tool over time
evidence.outcome: Silent-mode live performance versus original validation performance
evidence.effect: Live background AUC 0.78 vs original 0.75-0.81; AUPRC 0.41 vs prior 0.19-0.38
evidence.quote: The average AUC (0.78) during this follow-up is comparable to the original validations (AUCs ranging between 0.75 and 0.81), while the AUPRC (0.41) even is slightly higher (previous AUPRCs ranging between 0.19 and 0.38).

evidence.title: Development, deployment, and continuous monitoring of a machine learning model to predict respiratory failure in critically ill patients
evidence.outcome: Prospective silent-mode performance on live EHR data versus retrospective performance
evidence.effect: Over a 1-month silent-mode deployment (276 encounters), AUC 0.908, sensitivity 0.632, specificity 0.849, PPV 0.235, above the 0.85 PCCP threshold, so no fine-tuning was needed.
evidence.quote: The final model achieved a sensitivity of 0.632, specificity of 0.849, and PPV of 0.235.
evidence.sample_unit: ICU encounters (26,045 development, 276 prospective silent-mode, 35,534 MIMIC-IV)

commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen observational studies suggest that running a tool silently on live data can reveal performance drops, data feed failures, coding errors, and false triggers before outputs reach clinicians. No study compared go-live with and without a silent phase, so the effect on patient harm has not been measured.

perspectives.view: All 13 tests are observational, and eight used a prospective comparator. None compared deployments with and without a silent phase. The studies measure whether silent mode detects problems, which is an indirect outcome for patient harm. Findings point the same way, but small samples limit precision, such as 100 encounters with a sensitivity confidence interval of 66% to 99%.

Silent runs surfaced failures that may otherwise have reached care. One run exposed an EHR data feed outage, another found coding errors, and a third logged 73 false triggers. In one screening program, AI missed 8 cancers that human readers recalled. Across 12 laboratory models, prospective AUROC fell below retrospective estimates.

Live performance often matched testing. Sensitivity was 81.7% versus 82.0% in one study, 91% versus 92% in another, and 85.29% in a third with similar testing values. A shadow AUC of 0.78 fell within the original 0.75 to 0.81. Local predeployment evaluation agreed with postdeployment value for 10 of 12 tasks. CT angiography shadow testing found setting-specific metrics.

Silent phases took time and reviewer effort. Reported runs lasted from 1 month to 77 days. One screening program reviewed 1,135 discordant cases and found 1 additional recall. None of the studies reported staffing hours or costs, so the resources needed for a silent phase remain unknown.

One ICU deployment judged 1 month of silent-mode results (AUC 0.908) against a 0.85 threshold in a predetermined change control plan and concluded that no fine-tuning was needed. This suggests that silent-mode data can feed formal change-control decisions. The regulatory discussion paper frames prospective scenario testing as something developers may do, not as a requirement.

No test reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Sites were in the United States, United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Singapore, and several studies did not report a setting. The endorsement for resource-limited hospitals rests on commentary, not on a test.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without a silent phase on patient harm, time to detecting failures, or cost. Evidence is also lacking on how long a silent phase should run, how many cases it needs, and which thresholds should trigger a decision not to go live.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the 13 tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A silent run in one population may therefore miss performance gaps that appear only in those groups. Health systems serving them would need to check subgroup results in their own silent phase.
